text: Which keyword is used to define a class in Java?
explanation:
class is correct because Java declares a new reference type with the class keyword. A class groups state and behavior together, and objects are created from that class as instances.

Example:

public class User {
    private String name;

    public User(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

text: Which method is the entry point of a standard Java application?
explanation:
main is correct because The JVM starts a standard standalone Java program by looking for a public static void main(String[] args) method. Without that signature, the program is not a normal application entry point.

Example:

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Application started");
    }
}

text: Which access modifier makes a member visible only within the same class?
explanation:
private is correct because A private member is visible only inside the class that declares it. This is a core encapsulation tool because outside code must use public methods instead of touching the field directly.

Example:

public class Account {
    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        balance += amount;
    }
}

text: Which collection stores elements in insertion order and allows duplicates?
explanation:
List is correct because A List preserves insertion order and allows duplicate values. That makes it a better fit than Set when order matters or repeated values are valid.

Example:

List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();
tags.add("java");
tags.add("java");
System.out.println(tags); // [java, java]

text: Which keyword is used to inherit from a class in Java?
explanation:
extends is correct because Java uses extends when one class inherits state or behavior from another class. The subclass can reuse the parent implementation and optionally override selected methods.

Example:

class User {
    String role() {
        return "USER";
    }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    @Override
    String role() {
        return "ADMIN";
    }
}

text: Which keyword is used when a class follows an interface contract?
explanation:
implements is correct because A class uses implements to promise that it will provide the methods declared by an interface. This is how Java models contracts separately from inheritance of a concrete class.

Example:

interface MessageSender {
    void send(String message);
}

class EmailSender implements MessageSender {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println(message);
    }
}

text: Which statement is used to handle exceptions in Java?
explanation:
try-catch is correct because A try-catch block wraps code that may fail and lets Java recover or respond when an exception is thrown. It keeps error-handling logic explicit instead of silently ignoring failures.

Example:

try {
    int value = Integer.parseInt("abc");
} catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
    System.out.println("Input was not a valid number");
}

text: Which type is commonly used for true or false values in Java?
explanation:
boolean is correct because The primitive type boolean stores only true or false. It is the correct type for flags, conditions, and method results that answer yes/no questions.

Example:

boolean active = true;
if (active) {
    System.out.println("User is active");
}

text: Which keyword is used to create a new object in Java?
explanation:
new is correct because The new keyword allocates memory for an object and calls its constructor. Without new, you only have a class definition, not an actual instance to work with.

Example:

User user = new User("Mia");
System.out.println(user);

text: Which class is commonly used for dynamic arrays in Java?
explanation:
ArrayList is correct because ArrayList is the most common resizable-array implementation of List. It is a strong default when you need ordered elements and fast indexed reads.

Example:

List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
scores.add(10);
scores.add(20);
System.out.println(scores.get(1)); // 20

text: Which annotation marks a method that overrides a superclass method?
explanation:
@Override is correct because @Override tells the compiler that a method is intended to override a parent or interface method. It improves safety because the compiler can catch signature mistakes immediately.

Example:

class User {
    public String toString() {
        return "User";
    }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "AdminUser";
    }
}

text: Which keyword prevents a variable from being reassigned after initialization?
explanation:
final is correct because final is used in Java to prevent reassignment or extension depending on context. For variables, it means the reference or value is assigned once; for classes, it prevents subclassing.

Example:

final String appName = "QuizApp";
// appName = "Other"; // compile error

text: Which primitive type is used for whole numbers in Java?
explanation:
int is correct because int is the standard 32-bit primitive for whole numbers in Java. Use it when fractional precision is not needed and the value range fits normal integer arithmetic.

Example:

int quantity = 42;
int total = quantity + 8;
System.out.println(total); // 50

text: Which primitive type is commonly used for decimal values in Java?
explanation:
double is correct because double stores floating-point values and is commonly used when decimal precision is needed. It is appropriate for measurements and calculations that are not strictly whole numbers.

Example:

double price = 19.99;
double total = price * 2;
System.out.println(total);

text: Which primitive type stores a single Unicode character in Java?
explanation:
char is correct because char stores one UTF-16 code unit and is used for a single character rather than a whole string. It is useful when you need to examine or compare one character at a time.

Example:

char grade = 'A';
if (grade == 'A') {
    System.out.println("Excellent");
}

text: Which keyword refers to the current object instance in Java?
explanation:
this is correct because this refers to the current object instance. It is commonly used to distinguish fields from constructor parameters or to call another instance method on the same object.

Example:

public class User {
    private String name;

    public User(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

text: Which keyword is used to call a superclass constructor or method?
explanation:
super is correct because super refers to the immediate parent class and is used to call parent constructors or parent method implementations. It is especially useful when a subclass extends existing behavior instead of replacing it entirely.

Example:

class User {
    User(String name) {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    AdminUser() {
        super("Admin");
    }
}

text: Which keyword indicates that a method does not return any value?
explanation:
void is correct because A method declared with void performs work but does not return a value to its caller. This is the right choice for actions such as logging, updating state, or printing output.

Example:

public void printSummary() {
    System.out.println("Summary generated");
}

text: Which statement exits a loop immediately in Java?
explanation:
break is correct because break exits the nearest loop or switch immediately. It is useful when continuing the loop no longer makes sense after a condition is met.

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i == 5) {
        break;
    }
    System.out.println(i);
}

text: Which statement skips the current loop iteration and moves to the next one?
explanation:
continue is correct because continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next one. It is useful when one condition should ignore a particular item but not end the whole loop.

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if (i == 2) {
        continue;
    }
    System.out.println(i);
}

text: Which class is commonly used for key-value storage in Java?
explanation:
HashMap is correct because HashMap stores key-value pairs and provides fast lookup by key in typical cases. It is one of the most common choices when you need to associate one value with another.

Example:

Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Mia", 90);
scores.put("Noah", 85);
System.out.println(scores.get("Mia"));

text: Which collection type does not allow duplicate elements?
explanation:
Set is correct because A Set does not allow duplicate elements, which makes it a good choice when uniqueness matters more than index-based access.

Example:

Set<String> roles = new HashSet<>();
roles.add("ADMIN");
roles.add("ADMIN");
System.out.println(roles.size()); // 1

text: Which implementation keeps elements sorted in natural order in a set?
explanation:
TreeSet is correct because TreeSet keeps unique elements sorted in their natural order or by a supplied comparator. It is useful when you need both uniqueness and sorted iteration.

Example:

Set<Integer> values = new TreeSet<>();
values.add(5);
values.add(1);
values.add(3);
System.out.println(values); // [1, 3, 5]

text: Which implementation keeps insertion order in a map?
explanation:
LinkedHashMap is correct because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order while still storing key-value pairs. It is helpful when order of iteration should match the order entries were added.

Example:

Map<String, Integer> order = new LinkedHashMap<>();
order.put("first", 1);
order.put("second", 2);
System.out.println(order.keySet()); // [first, second]

text: Which class is commonly used for thread-safe immutable text strings?
explanation:
String is correct because String represents immutable text in Java. Because strings cannot be changed after creation, they are thread-safe to share and safe to use as keys or values.

Example:

String greeting = "Hello";
String name = "Java";
System.out.println(greeting + " " + name);

text: Which class is commonly used for mutable string manipulation in single-threaded code?
explanation:
StringBuilder is correct because StringBuilder is designed for efficient mutable string construction in single-threaded code. It avoids creating many intermediate String objects when text is built step by step.

Example:

StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder();
builder.append("Java");
builder.append(" ");
builder.append("Quiz");
System.out.println(builder.toString());

text: Which class is similar to StringBuilder but synchronized for thread safety?
explanation:
StringBuffer is correct because StringBuffer is like StringBuilder but synchronized for thread-safe mutation. It is less common in modern code, but it is still the thread-safe mutable-string variant.

Example:

StringBuffer buffer = new StringBuffer();
buffer.append("safe");
buffer.append(" text");
System.out.println(buffer.toString());

text: Which operator concatenates strings in Java?
explanation:
+ is correct because The + operator concatenates strings by creating a new string containing both operands in sequence. It is convenient for simple text composition.

Example:

String firstName = "Ada";
String message = "Hello, " + firstName + "!";
System.out.println(message);

text: Which method compares two strings for exact content equality?
explanation:
equals() is correct because equals() compares logical content rather than object identity. For strings and domain objects, it answers whether two values should be treated as meaningfully equal.

Example:

String left = new String("java");
String right = new String("java");
System.out.println(left.equals(right)); // true

text: Which operator checks whether two references point to the same object?
explanation:
== is correct because == compares primitive values directly, but for objects it checks whether both references point to the exact same instance in memory. That is why it should not be used for logical string comparison.

Example:

String a = new String("java");
String b = new String("java");
System.out.println(a == b);      // false
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true

text: Which interface represents a functional interface often used with lambda expressions that takes no input and returns a value?
explanation:
Supplier is correct because Supplier<T> represents a function that takes no input and returns a value. It is useful when a value should be produced lazily, repeatedly, or by passing behavior around.

Example:

Supplier<String> tokenSupplier = () -> "token-" + System.currentTimeMillis();
System.out.println(tokenSupplier.get());

text: Which interface represents a functional interface that takes one input and returns no result?
explanation:
Consumer is correct because Consumer<T> takes one input and returns no result. It is commonly used for callbacks, printing, logging, or applying side effects to each value.

Example:

Consumer<String> printer = text -> System.out.println(text.toUpperCase());
printer.accept("java");

text: Which interface represents a boolean-valued function of one argument?
explanation:
Predicate is correct because Predicate<T> represents a function that returns true or false for one input. It is heavily used in filtering and validation logic.

Example:

Predicate<Integer> isEven = n -> n % 2 == 0;
System.out.println(isEven.test(4)); // true

text: Which interface represents a function from one type to another?
explanation:
Function is correct because Function<T, R> transforms one value into another. It is common in stream mapping and other functional-style pipelines.

Example:

Function<String, Integer> length = text -> text.length();
System.out.println(length.apply("java")); // 4

text: Which Java feature allows passing behavior as data using concise syntax?
explanation:
Lambda expressions is correct because Lambda expressions let Java treat behavior like data by writing small inline implementations of functional interfaces. They reduce boilerplate compared with anonymous inner classes.

Example:

List<String> names = List.of("mia", "noah");
names.forEach(name -> System.out.println(name.toUpperCase()));

text: Which stream operation transforms each element into another value?
explanation:
map is correct because The stream operation map transforms each element into another value and returns a new stream. It is the right choice when the shape of each item changes.

Example:

List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Linus");
List<Integer> lengths = names.stream()
    .map(String::length)
    .toList();

text: Which stream operation keeps only elements that match a condition?
explanation:
filter is correct because The stream operation filter keeps only elements that satisfy a condition. It is used when some items should be dropped from further processing.

Example:

List<Integer> values = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4);
List<Integer> even = values.stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .toList();

text: Which stream terminal operation accumulates elements into a single result?
explanation:
reduce is correct because The terminal operation reduce combines stream elements into one accumulated result. It is useful for sums, products, and other fold-style computations.

Example:

int total = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).stream()
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum);
System.out.println(total); // 10

text: Which collector is commonly used to gather stream results into a list?
explanation:
Collectors.toList() is correct because Collectors.toList() is a collector used to gather stream results into a list. It is common when a stream pipeline should end as a materialized collection.

Example:

List<String> upper = List.of("a", "b").stream()
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

text: Which Java package contains List, Set, Map, and related collection interfaces?
explanation:
java.util is correct because java.util is the package that contains the core collection interfaces and many utility classes such as List, Set, Map, and Scanner.

Example:

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

List<String> languages = new ArrayList<>();

text: Which exception is unchecked in Java?
explanation:
NullPointerException is correct because NullPointerException is unchecked because it extends RuntimeException. The compiler does not force callers to catch or declare it, even though it may happen at runtime.

Example:

String text = null;
// Throws NullPointerException at runtime:
System.out.println(text.length());

text: Which keyword is used to declare that a method may throw checked exceptions?
explanation:
throws is correct because The throws keyword declares that a method may pass checked exceptions to its caller. It makes exception contracts explicit in the method signature.

Example:

public String readFile(Path path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(path);
}

text: Which statement is used to explicitly raise an exception in Java code?
explanation:
throw is correct because The throw statement explicitly raises an exception object. Use it when code detects an invalid state or input that should stop normal execution.

Example:

if (amount < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
}

text: Which block runs whether or not an exception occurs?
explanation:
finally is correct because A finally block runs whether or not an exception is thrown, making it useful for cleanup that must happen either way.

Example:

try {
    System.out.println("work");
} finally {
    System.out.println("cleanup");
}

text: Which class is the root of the Java exception hierarchy?
explanation:
Throwable is correct because Throwable is the root of Java’s throwable hierarchy. Both Exception and Error ultimately derive from it.

Example:

try {
    throw new Exception("failure");
} catch (Throwable t) {
    System.out.println(t.getMessage());
}

text: Which keyword prevents a class from being subclassed?
explanation:
final is correct because when applied to a class, final prevents inheritance. This is useful when the class design should stay closed to subclass behavior changes.

Example:

final class Utility {
}

// class Child extends Utility {} // compile error

text: Which keyword indicates a member belongs to the class rather than an instance?
explanation:
static is correct because static means a member belongs to the class itself instead of one object instance. Static members are shared and can be accessed without creating an object.

Example:

public class MathUtil {
    public static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

int result = MathUtil.add(2, 3);

text: Which access modifier allows visibility within the same package and subclasses?
explanation:
protected is correct because protected makes a member visible to code in the same package and to subclasses, even when those subclasses are in a different package.

Example:

class User {
    protected String name;
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    void printName() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

text: Which access level is used when no modifier is declared on a member?
explanation:
package-private is correct because Package-private access is what Java uses when no modifier is declared. The member is visible only inside the same package, which is useful for internal collaboration between classes.

Example:

class PackageHelper {
    void assist() {
        System.out.println("Same-package access only");
    }
}

text: Which Java feature allows one method name to have multiple parameter lists?
explanation:
Method overloading is correct because Method overloading means the same method name is reused with different parameter lists. It improves readability when operations are conceptually the same but accept different inputs.

Example:

class MathUtil {
    int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
    int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }
}

text: Which Java feature allows a subclass to provide a different implementation of a superclass method?
explanation:
Method overriding is correct because Method overriding happens when a subclass provides its own implementation of a method declared in a parent class. This is how polymorphism customizes inherited behavior.

Example:

class User {
    String role() { return "USER"; }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    @Override
    String role() { return "ADMIN"; }
}

text: Which concept bundles data and methods together and restricts direct access to internals?
explanation:
Encapsulation is correct because Encapsulation means keeping fields and related methods together while restricting direct outside access to internal state. It protects invariants and makes code easier to evolve safely.

Example:

class Account {
    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0) {
            balance += amount;
        }
    }
}

text: Which OOP principle focuses on exposing essential behavior while hiding implementation details?
explanation:
Abstraction is correct because Abstraction focuses on exposing what an object can do while hiding how it does it. Interfaces and abstract classes are common Java tools for this idea.

Example:

interface PaymentService {
    void pay(double amount);
}

class CardPaymentService implements PaymentService {
    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Paid " + amount);
    }
}

text: Which keyword is used to define an abstract class?
explanation:
abstract is correct because The abstract keyword marks a class or method as incomplete and intended to be extended. An abstract class can provide shared code while requiring subclasses to implement specific behavior.

Example:

abstract class Report {
    abstract String type();
}

class SalesReport extends Report {
    String type() { return "sales"; }
}

text: Which type can contain abstract methods and constants and be implemented by classes?
explanation:
Interface is correct because An interface defines a contract that classes can implement. It is useful when multiple classes should share the same API without sharing the same inheritance tree.

Example:

interface Notifier {
    void send(String message);
}

class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println(message);
    }
}

text: Which Java keyword is used to define named constants in an enum type?
explanation:
enum is correct because The enum keyword defines a fixed set of named constants. Enums improve readability and type safety compared with raw strings or integers for well-known categories.

Example:

enum Status {
    NEW, IN_PROGRESS, DONE
}

Status status = Status.NEW;

text: Which Java type is useful for immutable data carriers with generated methods like equals and hashCode?
explanation:
record is correct because A record is ideal for immutable data carriers because Java generates useful members like a constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString automatically.

Example:

public record UserDto(Long id, String name) {
}

UserDto dto = new UserDto(1L, "Mia");

text: Which method is inherited from Object and often overridden for readable object output?
explanation:
toString() is correct because toString() is inherited from Object and is commonly overridden to produce a readable string form of an object. This improves logging and debugging output.

Example:

class User {
    private final String name = "Mia";

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "User{name='" + name + "'}";
    }
}

text: Which method is commonly overridden to define logical equality between objects?
explanation:
equals() is correct because overriding equals() lets a class define when two objects should be considered logically equal instead of relying on reference identity. This is essential for domain objects, collections, and testing.

Example:

class User {
    private final String email;

    User(String email) {
        this.email = email;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        return obj instanceof User other && email.equals(other.email);
    }
}

text: Which method should usually be overridden consistently with equals()?
explanation:
hashCode() is correct because hashCode() should be consistent with equals() so hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet behave correctly.

Example:

class User {
    private final String email;

    User(String email) {
        this.email = email;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof User other && email.equals(other.email);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return email.hashCode();
    }
}

text: Which Java package contains file and stream I/O classes like File and InputStream?
explanation:
java.io is correct because java.io contains classic input/output classes such as streams, readers, writers, and File. It is the traditional package for byte and character I/O.

Example:

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));

text: Which Java package contains the newer NIO file APIs such as Path and Files?
explanation:
java.nio.file is correct because java.nio.file contains the modern file APIs such as Path and Files. It is usually preferred for clearer and more powerful file operations.

Example:

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

String text = Files.readString(Path.of("notes.txt"));

text: Which class represents a filesystem path in the NIO API?
explanation:
Path is correct because Path represents a filesystem path in the NIO API. It is more flexible and modern than using raw string paths everywhere.

Example:

Path report = Path.of("reports", "today.txt");
System.out.println(report);

text: Which utility class contains static methods for copying and reading files in NIO?
explanation:
Files is correct because Files is a utility class containing many static methods for reading, writing, copying, and inspecting files in the NIO API.

Example:

Path file = Path.of("notes.txt");
Files.writeString(file, "Hello Java");
String content = Files.readString(file);

text: Which class is commonly used to read text input from the console or other streams token by token?
explanation:
Scanner is correct because Scanner reads tokenized input conveniently from the console or another stream. It is often used for beginner-friendly parsing of numbers and words.

Example:

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = scanner.nextInt();
System.out.println(age);

text: Which class is commonly used for buffered character input?
explanation:
BufferedReader is correct because BufferedReader is commonly used for efficient character input, especially line-by-line reading from text sources.

Example:

try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("data.txt"))) {
    String line = reader.readLine();
}

text: Which keyword ensures a resource is automatically closed at the end of a block?
explanation:
try-with-resources is correct because try-with-resources automatically closes resources at the end of the block, even when an exception occurs. It makes I/O code safer and less verbose.

Example:

try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("data.txt"))) {
    System.out.println(reader.readLine());
}

text: Which interface must a resource implement to be used in try-with-resources?
explanation:
AutoCloseable is correct because A resource used in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable so Java knows it has a close() method to call automatically.

Example:

class ReportWriter implements AutoCloseable {
    public void close() {
        System.out.println("closed");
    }
}

text: Which package contains classes for modern date and time handling such as LocalDate?
explanation:
java.time is correct because java.time is the modern Java date-time API package. It is clearer, more immutable, and safer than older date APIs.

Example:

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();

text: Which class represents a date without a time zone in java.time?
explanation:
LocalDate is correct because LocalDate represents a calendar date without a time or time zone. Use it for birthdays, due dates, or business dates.

Example:

LocalDate releaseDate = LocalDate.of(2026, 6, 3);
System.out.println(releaseDate);

text: Which class represents a date and time without a time zone in java.time?
explanation:
LocalDateTime is correct because LocalDateTime stores both date and time but no time zone. It is useful for local scheduling values that are not tied to one exact instant worldwide.

Example:

LocalDateTime meeting = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 6, 3, 14, 30);
System.out.println(meeting);

text: Which class represents a moment on the UTC timeline?
explanation:
Instant is correct because Instant represents a precise moment on the UTC timeline. It is a strong choice for timestamps that must be globally comparable.

Example:

Instant createdAt = Instant.now();
System.out.println(createdAt);

text: Which class represents a zone identifier like America/New_York?
explanation:
ZoneId is correct because ZoneId represents a region-based time zone such as America/New_York. It is used when converting between local date-times and actual instants.

Example:

ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of("America/New_York");
System.out.println(zone);

text: Which Java class is commonly used to create and run a new thread directly?
explanation:
Thread is correct because Thread is the core JDK class for creating and running a new thread directly. It is low-level compared with executors but still important to understand.

Example:

Thread worker = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Working"));
worker.start();

text: Which interface is often implemented when a task should run in a thread and return no result?
explanation:
Runnable is correct because Runnable represents a task with no return value. It is commonly passed to threads or executors when you only need work to run, not a result to come back.

Example:

Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("Task running");
new Thread(task).start();

text: Which interface is similar to Runnable but can return a value and throw checked exceptions?
explanation:
Callable is correct because Callable<T> is like Runnable but it can return a value and throw checked exceptions. It is commonly used with executor services.

Example:

Callable<Integer> task = () -> 40 + 2;
Future<Integer> future = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().submit(task);

text: Which concurrency utility manages pools of worker threads?
explanation:
ExecutorService is correct because ExecutorService manages a pool of worker threads and is usually preferred over manually creating many Thread objects. It gives better lifecycle and concurrency control.

Example:

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
executor.submit(() -> System.out.println("job"));
executor.shutdown();

text: Which method on ExecutorService initiates an orderly shutdown?
explanation:
shutdown() is correct because shutdown() tells an ExecutorService to stop accepting new tasks while letting already submitted work finish normally.

Example:

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
executor.submit(() -> System.out.println("done"));
executor.shutdown();

text: Which class is commonly used for thread-safe incrementing counters without explicit synchronization?
explanation:
AtomicInteger is correct because AtomicInteger supports thread-safe atomic updates without explicit synchronization blocks. It is useful for counters shared across multiple threads.

Example:

AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
counter.incrementAndGet();
System.out.println(counter.get());

text: Which keyword in Java helps ensure visibility of variable updates across threads?
explanation:
volatile is correct because volatile helps ensure that writes to a field by one thread are visible to other threads reading that field. It is about visibility, not full compound-operation safety.

Example:

class FlagHolder {
    private volatile boolean running = true;

    void stop() {
        running = false;
    }
}

text: Which keyword is used to enforce that only one thread at a time can execute a method or block?
explanation:
synchronized is correct because synchronized ensures that only one thread at a time executes a guarded method or block for the same monitor. It is commonly used to protect shared mutable state.

Example:

class Counter {
    private int value;

    public synchronized void increment() {
        value++;
    }
}

text: Which exception may be thrown when Thread.sleep() is interrupted?
explanation:
InterruptedException is correct because InterruptedException can be thrown when a sleeping, waiting, or blocking thread is interrupted. Good Java code usually handles it by restoring the interrupt or stopping work appropriately.

Example:

try {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
} catch (InterruptedException ex) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

text: Which JDK collection implementation is thread-safe for non-blocking concurrent maps?
explanation:
ConcurrentHashMap is correct because ConcurrentHashMap is a thread-safe map implementation designed for concurrent access without one global lock around every operation.

Example:

Map<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.put("java", 1);
counts.merge("java", 1, Integer::sum);

text: Which class loader method is commonly used to read a classpath resource as a stream?
explanation:
getResourceAsStream() is correct because getResourceAsStream() is commonly used to read a classpath resource such as a file packaged inside src/main/resources. It returns an input stream for that resource.

Example:

try (InputStream input = App.class.getResourceAsStream("/config.properties")) {
    Properties props = new Properties();
    props.load(input);
}

text: Which Java mechanism allows checking an object’s type before casting?
explanation:
instanceof is correct because instanceof checks whether an object is of a given type before casting. It helps avoid invalid casts and makes type-dependent logic safer.

Example:

Object value = "java";
if (value instanceof String text) {
    System.out.println(text.toUpperCase());
}

text: Which wrapper class corresponds to the primitive type int?
explanation:
Integer is correct because Integer is the wrapper class for the primitive type int. It is needed when Java requires an object instead of a primitive, such as in generics or collections.

Example:

List<Integer> scores = List.of(10, 20, 30);
Integer first = scores.get(0);

text: Which Java feature automatically converts an int to an Integer when needed?
explanation:
Autoboxing is correct because Autoboxing is Java’s automatic conversion from a primitive like int to its wrapper type such as Integer. This is especially common in collections and generic APIs.

Example:

Integer score = 10; // int -> Integer
List<Integer> values = new ArrayList<>();
values.add(5);

text: Which Java feature automatically converts an Integer to an int when needed?
explanation:
Unboxing is correct because Unboxing is Java’s automatic conversion from a wrapper like Integer back to a primitive such as int. It is convenient but can throw NullPointerException if the wrapper is null.

Example:

Integer boxed = 42;
int value = boxed; // Integer -> int
System.out.println(value);

text: Which static method commonly converts a String to an int?
explanation:
Integer.parseInt() is correct because Integer.parseInt() converts a numeric string into an int. It is the usual choice when reading whole-number input from text.

Example:

String raw = "123";
int value = Integer.parseInt(raw);
System.out.println(value + 1); // 124

text: Which class is often used to sort collections with custom comparison logic?
explanation:
Comparator is correct because A Comparator defines custom comparison logic outside the class being sorted. It is useful when the class itself does not own a single natural ordering or when multiple orderings are needed.

Example:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Mia", "Alexander", "Noah"));
names.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

text: Which interface allows a class to define its natural ordering?
explanation:
Comparable is correct because Comparable lets a class define its natural ordering by implementing compareTo(). Collections can then sort those objects without an external comparator.

Example:

class User implements Comparable<User> {
    private final String name;

    User(String name) { this.name = name; }

    public int compareTo(User other) {
        return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
    }
}

text: Which method is defined by Comparable?
explanation:
compareTo() is correct because compareTo() is the method required by Comparable and defines how one object orders itself relative to another. Negative, zero, and positive results indicate before, equal, or after.

Example:

public int compareTo(User other) {
    return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
}

text: Which interface allows a class to be the target of a for-each loop?
explanation:
Iterable is correct because Iterable allows an object to participate in the enhanced for-each loop. If a type can produce an iterator, Java can iterate over it naturally.

Example:

class NameCollection implements Iterable<String> {
    public Iterator<String> iterator() {
        return List.of("A", "B").iterator();
    }
}

text: Which method is required by the Iterable interface?
explanation:
iterator() is correct because iterator() is the method required by Iterable. It returns an Iterator that walks through the elements in sequence.

Example:

Iterable<String> values = List.of("x", "y");
Iterator<String> iterator = values.iterator();

text: Which Iterator method checks whether more elements remain?
explanation:
hasNext() is correct because hasNext() checks whether an iterator still has another element available. It prevents calling next() past the end of the sequence.

Example:

Iterator<Integer> iterator = List.of(1, 2).iterator();
while (iterator.hasNext()) {
    System.out.println(iterator.next());
}

text: Which Iterator method returns the next element in a sequence?
explanation:
next() is correct because next() returns the next element from an iterator. It advances the iterator each time it is called.

Example:

Iterator<String> iterator = List.of("A", "B").iterator();
String first = iterator.next();

text: Which class is commonly used for optional return values that may be absent?
explanation:
Optional is correct because Optional<T> represents a value that may or may not be present. It encourages callers to handle absence explicitly instead of assuming null is always safe.

Example:

Optional<String> name = Optional.ofNullable(findName());
name.ifPresent(System.out::println);

text: Which Optional method returns true when a value is present?
explanation:
isPresent() is correct because isPresent() returns true when an Optional contains a value. It can be useful, though methods like ifPresent or orElse are often more expressive.

Example:

Optional<String> name = Optional.of("Java");
if (name.isPresent()) {
    System.out.println(name.get());
}

text: Which Optional method supplies a fallback value if none is present?
explanation:
orElse() is correct because orElse() returns the wrapped value when present or a fallback when absent. It is useful for defaulting without writing explicit null checks.

Example:

Optional<String> nickname = Optional.empty();
String result = nickname.orElse("Guest");
System.out.println(result);

text: Which keyword is used to write a switch expression arm in modern Java syntax?
explanation:
yield is correct because In a switch expression, yield returns a value from a block-style case arm. It is used when the arm needs multiple statements before producing its final result.

Example:

int day = 6;
String type = switch (day) {
    case 6, 7 -> {
        System.out.println("Weekend selected");
        yield "WEEKEND";
    }
    default -> "WEEKDAY";
};

text: Which Java feature reduces boilerplate in switch statements by using arrow labels?
explanation:
Switch expressions is correct because Switch expressions reduce boilerplate by letting each arm produce a value directly with arrow syntax. They are often clearer and less error-prone than old fall-through switch statements.

Example:

int score = 2;
String label = switch (score) {
    case 1 -> "LOW";
    case 2 -> "MEDIUM";
    default -> "HIGH";
};

text: Which keyword is used to inherit behavior from a parent class constructor chain?
explanation:
super is correct because super refers to the immediate parent class and is used to call parent constructors or parent method implementations. It is especially useful when a subclass extends existing behavior instead of replacing it entirely.

Example:

class User {
    User(String name) {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    AdminUser() {
        super("Admin");
    }
}

text: Which package is imported automatically into every Java source file?
explanation:
java.lang is correct because java.lang is imported automatically into every Java source file. That is why classes like String, Object, and System can be used without an explicit import.

Example:

String text = "Java";
System.out.println(text.length());

text: Which class in java.lang is the parent of all Java classes?
explanation:
Object is correct because Object is the root parent of all Java classes. Every reference type inherits methods such as toString(), equals(), and hashCode() from it.

Example:

class User {
}

Object value = new User();
System.out.println(value.toString());

text: Which class provides access to standard output, standard error, and environment info?
explanation:
System is correct because System provides access to core platform features such as standard output, standard error, time, properties, and environment integration.

Example:

System.out.println("Hello");
System.err.println("Something went wrong");

text: Which field is commonly used to write to standard output?
explanation:
System.out is correct because System.out is the standard output stream used for normal console printing. It is usually the first place beginners write messages in Java programs.

Example:

System.out.println("Quiz started");

text: Which class is commonly used to execute external operating system commands?
explanation:
ProcessBuilder is correct because ProcessBuilder is commonly used to launch external operating-system commands from Java. It gives more control than the older Runtime.exec() style.

Example:

ProcessBuilder builder = new ProcessBuilder("echo", "Hello from Java");
Process process = builder.start();

text: Which Java keyword allows a subclass method to call the same method implementation from its parent?
explanation:
super is correct because super refers to the immediate parent class and is used to call parent constructors or parent method implementations. It is especially useful when a subclass extends existing behavior instead of replacing it entirely.

Example:

class User {
    User(String name) {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

class AdminUser extends User {
    AdminUser() {
        super("Admin");
    }
}

text: Which package contains annotations like @Override and @Deprecated?
explanation:
java.lang is correct because java.lang is imported automatically into every Java source file. That is why classes like String, Object, and System can be used without an explicit import.

Example:

String text = "Java";
System.out.println(text.length());

text: Which annotation marks an API element as discouraged for use?
explanation:
@Deprecated is correct because @Deprecated marks an API element as discouraged for new use. IDEs and compilers can then warn callers that a better replacement should be preferred.

Example:

@Deprecated
public void oldMethod() {
    System.out.println("Use newMethod instead");
}

text: Which annotation indicates an interface is intended to have exactly one abstract method?
explanation:
@FunctionalInterface is correct because @FunctionalInterface indicates that an interface is intended to have exactly one abstract method, making it suitable for lambdas and method references.

Example:

@FunctionalInterface
interface Formatter {
    String format(String text);
}

text: Which Java feature lets subclasses share code from a common parent class?
explanation:
Inheritance is correct because Inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields or methods from a common parent class and optionally specialize behavior. It is one of the core OOP mechanisms for sharing code.

Example:

class Animal {
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
}

text: What does a Java class typically define?
explanation: State and behavior for objects is correct because a class groups fields and methods together as a blueprint for creating objects in Java.

text: What is the primary purpose of a Java interface?
choices: To define a contract of methods
explanation: To define a contract of methods is correct because an interface describes what implementing classes must provide without requiring shared concrete state.

text: When is an abstract class most useful in Java?
choices: When shared base behavior should be reused but direct instantiation should be prevented
When every field must be static
When objects should never inherit behavior
explanation: When shared base behavior should be reused but direct instantiation should be prevented is correct because abstract classes can contain common implementation while forcing subclasses to complete the design.

text: Which OOP concept is mainly achieved by hiding fields behind methods?
explanation: Encapsulation is correct because Java encourages protecting internal state and exposing controlled access through methods such as getters, setters, or domain operations.

text: What is method overloading in Java?
choices: Using the same method name with different parameter lists
Replacing a parent method with the exact same signature
Declaring duplicate methods with identical parameters
explanation: Using the same method name with different parameter lists is correct because overloaded methods are distinguished by their argument types or counts at compile time.

text: What is method overriding in Java?
choices: Providing a new implementation of an inherited method with the same signature
Creating methods with different parameter counts
explanation: Providing a new implementation of an inherited method with the same signature is correct because overriding lets a subclass specialize behavior defined by its parent or interface.

text: Which example best demonstrates polymorphism in Java?
choices: A parent reference holding a child object and calling an overridden method
A method returning two primitive values
A class with only static fields
explanation: A parent reference holding a child object and calling an overridden method is correct because runtime dispatch allows the child implementation to execute through the parent type.

text: What is the main role of a constructor in Java?
explanation: To initialize a new object is correct because constructors run during object creation and commonly assign required state.

text: What happens if a class declares no constructor at all?
choices: Java provides a default no-argument constructor
explanation: Java provides a default no-argument constructor is correct because the compiler adds one only when no constructor is explicitly declared.

text: What access level does a member have when no modifier is written in Java?
explanation: Package-private is correct because a member with no access modifier is visible to other classes in the same package only.

text: What does the protected access modifier allow?
choices: Access from the same package and from subclasses
Access only from the same class
explanation: Access from the same package and from subclasses is correct because protected is broader than private but narrower than public.

text: Which access modifier makes a class member visible from any package?
explanation: public is correct because public members are accessible anywhere the declaring type is visible.

text: Which modifier is most appropriate for a field that should be hidden from all other classes?
explanation: private is correct because it restricts direct access to the declaring class and supports strong encapsulation.

text: What does the static keyword indicate for a field or method?
choices: It belongs to the class rather than to each instance
It can be changed only once
explanation: It belongs to the class rather than to each instance is correct because static members are shared at the type level.

text: What does declaring a method as final prevent?
choices: Calling the method from other classes
explanation: Overriding in subclasses is correct because a final method keeps its implementation fixed throughout the inheritance chain.

text: What is the effect of declaring a class as final?
explanation: The class cannot be subclassed is correct because final stops inheritance for that type.

text: What does the synchronized keyword provide?
choices: Mutual exclusion for a guarded method or block
explanation: Mutual exclusion for a guarded method or block is correct because synchronized code uses a monitor so only one thread at a time can enter for the same lock.

text: Which keyword marks a field so it is skipped during default serialization?
explanation: transient is correct because transient fields are ignored by Java's default object serialization mechanism.

text: What problem does volatile mainly address in Java concurrency?
explanation: Visibility of writes between threads is correct because volatile helps one thread observe another thread's latest value updates.

text: Which operator checks whether an object is of a given type before casting?
explanation: instanceof is correct because it safely tests runtime type compatibility before a cast is performed.

text: Which collection is usually the default choice for an ordered, resizable list with fast indexed access?
explanation: ArrayList is correct because it stores elements in insertion order and offers efficient random access by index.

text: Which List implementation is often chosen when frequent insertions or removals happen at the ends?
explanation: LinkedList is correct because it is node-based and can be suitable for certain insertion or removal patterns, though it is usually slower for indexed access.

text: Which collection stores key-value pairs without guaranteeing iteration order?
explanation: HashMap is correct because it is a common map implementation optimized for fast lookup and does not preserve insertion or sorted order.

text: Which Map implementation preserves insertion order?
explanation: LinkedHashMap is correct because it links entries to keep iteration order aligned with insertion order by default.

text: Which Map implementation keeps keys sorted according to natural order or a Comparator?
explanation: TreeMap is correct because it stores entries in a sorted tree structure rather than hash buckets.

text: Which collection is designed to store unique elements only?
explanation: HashSet is correct because sets reject duplicate elements and HashSet is the common hash-based implementation.

text: Which Set implementation keeps insertion order while still preventing duplicates?
explanation: LinkedHashSet is correct because it combines set uniqueness with predictable insertion-order iteration.

text: Which Set implementation keeps elements sorted?
explanation: TreeSet is correct because it stores unique values in sorted order using a tree-based structure.

text: Which interface represents a collection intended for processing elements in FIFO style?
explanation: Queue is correct because the Queue interface models elements that are typically inserted at one end and removed from another.

text: Which interface supports adding and removing elements from both ends of a collection?
explanation: Deque is correct because a double-ended queue supports operations at both the front and the back.

text: What happens when put() is called on a HashMap with a key that already exists?
choices: The map throws an error every time
explanation: The old value is replaced is correct because a map cannot contain duplicate keys, so the new value becomes the mapping for that key.

text: Which Map method returns a fallback value when a key is absent?
explanation: getOrDefault() is correct because it avoids a separate null check when a map lookup might miss.

text: Which Map method is useful for lazily creating and storing a value only when a key is missing?
explanation: computeIfAbsent() is correct because it calculates a value only when no mapping is already present for the key.

text: Which Iterator method removes the current element safely during iteration?
explanation: remove() is correct because it removes the last element returned by the iterator in a way that stays consistent with iteration.

text: Which method is commonly used to sort a List in place in modern Java?
explanation: sort() is correct because List.sort() sorts the list using natural order or a supplied comparator.

text: Which interface is used to define custom sorting logic outside a class?
explanation: Comparator is correct because it lets code provide alternate ordering strategies without modifying the type being sorted.

text: Which statement about String in Java is true?
explanation: String is immutable is correct because once a String is created, its contents cannot be changed.

text: Which class is preferred for building text efficiently in single-threaded code?
explanation: StringBuilder is correct because it provides mutable character storage without the synchronization cost of StringBuffer.

text: Which class provides a thread-safe mutable sequence of characters?
explanation: StringBuffer is correct because it is synchronized and intended for mutable string operations in shared-thread scenarios.

text: Which String method extracts part of a string?
explanation: substring() is correct because it returns a new String containing a selected range of characters.

text: Which String method removes leading and trailing whitespace in basic Java usage?
explanation: trim() is correct because it returns a new string with surrounding whitespace removed.

text: Which method should usually be used to compare String contents?
explanation: equals() is correct because it compares logical text content rather than object identity.

text: Which String method compares text while ignoring letter case?
explanation: equalsIgnoreCase() is correct because it checks whether two strings have the same letters regardless of uppercase or lowercase differences.

text: Which String method returns the character at a given index?
explanation: charAt() is correct because it retrieves the UTF-16 code unit at a zero-based position.

text: Which String method breaks text into parts using a delimiter pattern?
explanation: split() is correct because it returns an array of substrings based on a regular-expression delimiter.

text: Which String method returns a new string with matching text substituted?
explanation: replace() is correct because String operations produce new values rather than mutating the original text.

text: Which method is commonly used to build a formatted String value?
explanation: String.format() is correct because it combines a format pattern and arguments into a new string.

text: Which String method added in Java 11 checks whether text is empty or contains only whitespace?
explanation: isBlank() is correct because Java 11 added it to detect strings that have no non-whitespace characters.

text: Which String method added in Java 11 repeats the same text multiple times?
explanation: repeat() is correct because Java 11 introduced it for concise repetition of string content.

text: Which String method added in Java 11 returns a stream of lines from text?
explanation: lines() is correct because it produces a lazy stream of line values from the string content.

text: Which abstract class is the base for reading raw bytes in Java I/O?
explanation: InputStream is correct because it is the core byte-input abstraction in the Java I/O API.

text: What is the role of InputStreamReader in Java I/O?
choices: It converts bytes from an InputStream into characters
It writes characters to a file
explanation: It converts bytes from an InputStream into characters is correct because InputStreamReader bridges byte streams and character streams using a character set.

text: Which class is commonly wrapped around a Reader to read text efficiently line by line?
explanation: BufferedReader is correct because it buffers input and provides methods like readLine() for convenient text reading.

text: Why is BufferedInputStream often used?
choices: To reduce expensive underlying read calls by buffering bytes
explanation: To reduce expensive underlying read calls by buffering bytes is correct because buffering improves efficiency when many small reads occur.

text: Which stream class is typically used to read raw bytes from a file?
explanation: FileInputStream is correct because it opens a file as a byte-based input stream.

text: Which Java feature automatically closes I/O resources at the end of a block?
explanation: try-with-resources is correct because resources that implement AutoCloseable are closed automatically when the block finishes.

text: What value does read() typically return when an InputStream reaches the end of the stream?
explanation: -1 is correct because byte and character read methods commonly signal end-of-stream with a negative result.

text: Which method forces buffered output to be written immediately?
explanation: flush() is correct because it pushes buffered data to the underlying destination without necessarily closing the stream.

text: Which abstract class is the base for writing raw bytes in Java?
explanation: OutputStream is correct because it is the primary abstraction for byte output.

text: Which abstract class is the base for writing character data in Java?
explanation: Writer is correct because it represents character-oriented output instead of raw byte output.

text: Which Thread method actually starts a new thread of execution?
explanation: start() is correct because it asks the JVM to create a separate execution path that will invoke run().

text: What is the purpose of the run() method in a Thread or Runnable?
choices: It contains the task code executed by the thread
It waits for another thread to finish
It shuts down the garbage collector
explanation: It contains the task code executed by the thread is correct because run() defines the work to perform when the thread is started.

text: Which Thread method lets one thread wait for another to finish?
explanation: join() is correct because it blocks until the target thread completes or the wait is otherwise interrupted or timed out.

text: Which Thread method pauses the current thread for a period of time?
explanation: sleep() is correct because it pauses the current thread without releasing any monitor it may already hold.

text: What does a Java monitor represent in synchronized code?
choices: The lock associated with an object or class
explanation: The lock associated with an object or class is correct because synchronized methods and blocks coordinate access through a monitor.

text: What does wait() do when called inside synchronized code on an object?
choices: It releases that object's monitor and waits
explanation: It releases that object's monitor and waits is correct because wait() suspends the thread until notification or interruption while giving up the lock.

text: What does notify() do in Java concurrency?
choices: It wakes one thread waiting on the same monitor
It wakes every thread in the JVM
It starts a new thread pool
It forces a context switch immediately
explanation: It wakes one thread waiting on the same monitor is correct because notification targets threads waiting on that object's monitor.

text: What does notifyAll() do in Java concurrency?
choices: It wakes all threads waiting on the same monitor
It unlocks every synchronized block in the program
explanation: It wakes all threads waiting on the same monitor is correct because all waiters on that object become eligible to compete for the lock again.

text: Which class provides an explicit lock API as an alternative to synchronized?
explanation: ReentrantLock is correct because it offers explicit lock and unlock control plus advanced features such as timed lock attempts.

text: Which interface is commonly used to manage a pool of worker threads?
explanation: ExecutorService is correct because it separates task submission from low-level thread creation and lifecycle management.

text: Which interface is like Runnable but can return a value and throw checked exceptions?
explanation: Callable is correct because its call() method can produce a result and declare checked exceptions.

text: Which type represents the result of an asynchronous computation submitted to an ExecutorService?
explanation: Future is correct because it can later provide the task result, completion state, or cancellation status.

text: Which class is commonly used for a thread-safe counter without using synchronized blocks?
explanation: AtomicInteger is correct because it supports atomic operations such as increment-and-get across threads.

text: Which Map implementation is designed for safe concurrent access by multiple threads?
explanation: ConcurrentHashMap is correct because it supports concurrent updates and reads more safely than a plain HashMap.

text: Where are most Java objects allocated at runtime?
explanation: Heap memory is correct because object instances generally live on the heap where garbage collection can manage them.

text: What is primarily stored on a thread's stack in Java?
explanation: Method frames and local variables is correct because each thread keeps its own call stack for active method execution.

text: What is the main job of the Java garbage collector?
choices: To reclaim memory from unreachable objects
To close all open files instantly
To compile source code at startup
explanation: To reclaim memory from unreachable objects is correct because the garbage collector identifies objects that can no longer be reached and frees their memory.

text: What is a common goal of the G1 garbage collector?
choices: Balancing throughput with lower pause times on large heaps
explanation: Balancing throughput with lower pause times on large heaps is correct because G1 divides the heap into regions and prioritizes predictable pause behavior.

text: What characterizes the Serial GC in Java?
choices: It uses a single thread for garbage collection work
It stores objects off-heap by default
explanation: It uses a single thread for garbage collection work is correct because Serial GC is simple and can suit small applications but is not ideal for large concurrent workloads.

text: What is the young generation in generational garbage collection mainly intended for?
explanation: Short-lived newly created objects is correct because many Java objects die young, so the collector optimizes for frequent reclamation there.

text: Why is finalize() generally discouraged in modern Java?
choices: It is unreliable and deprecated for object cleanup
It is required for every serializable class
explanation: It is unreliable and deprecated for object cleanup is correct because finalization timing is unpredictable and safer cleanup mechanisms are preferred.

text: What is true about a weak reference in Java?
choices: It does not prevent its referent from being garbage collected
It guarantees an object will stay in memory
It works only for primitive values
It is stronger than a normal reference
explanation: It does not prevent its referent from being garbage collected is correct because weak references are designed for structures such as caches where retention should be soft.

text: Which Java feature provides a concise way to declare immutable data carriers with generated accessors?
explanation: record is correct because records reduce boilerplate for transparent data-holding classes and are standard in recent Java versions.

text: What do sealed classes introduced in recent Java versions allow you to do?
choices: Restrict which classes are permitted to extend or implement a type
Force all fields to be private
explanation: Restrict which classes are permitted to extend or implement a type is correct because sealed hierarchies make inheritance boundaries explicit.

text: Which recent Java feature makes multi-line string literals easier to write?
explanation: Text blocks is correct because they allow readable multi-line string literals without heavy escaping.

text: What does the var keyword do in local variable declarations?
choices: It lets the compiler infer the local variable type
It creates a dynamically typed variable
It forces the type to be Object
explanation: It lets the compiler infer the local variable type is correct because var is local type inference, not dynamic typing.

text: Which HTTP API became a standard modern choice in Java 11?
explanation: HttpClient is correct because Java 11 standardized the newer HTTP client API for synchronous and asynchronous requests.

text: Which Files method added in recent Java versions reads an entire file into a String?
explanation: readString() is correct because Files.readString() offers a concise way to read whole text files.

text: What improvement does pattern matching for instanceof provide in modern Java?
choices: It combines type checking and typed binding in one step
It removes the need for classes
It makes casting slower but safer
explanation: It combines type checking and typed binding in one step is correct because successful instanceof checks can introduce a typed variable directly.

text: What is a key advantage of switch expressions in modern Java?
choices: They can return values directly with less boilerplate
They require fall-through in every case
explanation: They can return values directly with less boilerplate is correct because switch expressions make branching expressions clearer and reduce accidental fall-through.

text: Which interface marks a class as eligible for default Java object serialization?
explanation: Serializable is correct because it is the marker interface Java checks for standard object serialization support.

text: Why might a class declare a serialVersionUID field?
choices: To control serialization compatibility across versions
explanation: To control serialization compatibility across versions is correct because serialVersionUID identifies the expected serialized form of a class.

text: Which class is commonly used to write serialized objects to a stream?
explanation: ObjectOutputStream is correct because it writes Java object graphs using the serialization mechanism.

text: Which class is commonly used to read serialized objects from a stream?
explanation: ObjectInputStream is correct because it reconstructs previously serialized objects from an input stream.

text: How does Externalizable differ from Serializable?
choices: It requires the class to manually define how state is written and read
It works only for primitive fields
It skips constructors during deserialization only
It cannot be used with Object streams
explanation: It requires the class to manually define how state is written and read is correct because Externalizable gives explicit control through writeExternal and readExternal.

text: Which methods can a Serializable class define to customize default serialization behavior?
explanation: writeObject() and readObject() is correct because these special methods let a Serializable class intercept and customize its serialized form.

text: What is the intent of the Decorator pattern?
choices: To add behavior to an object dynamically by wrapping it
To enforce a single global instance
To visit every node in a tree automatically
To create objects only through reflection

text: What is the main goal of the Visitor pattern?
choices: To separate operations from the object structure they work on
To synchronize access to shared data
To serialize objects to JSON automatically

To force serialization on every object

text: What is the purpose of the Factory Method pattern?
